source_text: Plura prosequi quid est necesse uel sacrifioioram in ludis genera monstruosa describere, inter quae nonnumquam et homo fit hostia latrocinio sacerdotis, dum cruor etiam de iugalo calidus exceptus spumanti patera, dum adhuc feruet, et quasi sitienti idolo in faciem iactatus crudeliter propinatur, et inter uoluptates spectantium quorundam mors erogatur, ut per cruentum spectaculum saeuire discatur, quasi parum sit homini priuata sua rabies, nisi illam et publice discat. in poenam hominis fera rabida nutritur in deliciis, ut sub spectantium oculis crudelius insaniat. erudit artifex belluam, quae dementior fortasse fuisset, si non illam magister crudelior saeuire docuisset. ergo ut taceam quicquid latius idololatria probat, quam uana sunt ipsa. certamina, lites in coloribus, contentiones in curribus, fauores in honoribus, gaudere quod equus uelocior fuerit,. maerere quod pigrior, annos pecoris computare, consules nosse, aetates discere, prosapiam designare, auos ipsos atauosque memorare. quam hoc totum otiosum negotium, immo quam turpiter ignominiosum? hunc, inquam, memoriter totam equini generis sobolem computantem et sine offensa hunc locum magna uelocitate referentem, parentes Christi si perroges, nescit, aut infelicior si scit. quem si rursus perrogem quo ad illud spectaculum itinere peruenerit, confitebitur per lupanarium, per prostitutarum nuda corpora, per lubricam libidinem, per dedecus publicum, per uulgarem lasciuiam, per communem omnium contumeliam. cui ut non obiciam quod fortasse commisit, uidit tamen quod committendum non fuit et oculos ad idololatriae spectaculum per libibinem duxit: ausus secum sanctum in lupanar ducere, si potuisset, qui festinans ad spectaculum dimissus e dominico et adhuc gerens secum ut assolet eucharistiam inter corpora obscoena meretricum Christi sanctum corpus infidelis iste circumtulit plus damnationis meritus de itinere quam de spectaculi uoluptate.
thought_title: The circus route and the profaned Eucharist
orientation: Novatian is still attacking the circus games, now describing their cruelty and then the shameful route a Christian takes to reach them.
pass_a_gloss: Why is it necessary to pursue more things or to describe the monstrous kinds of sacrifices in the games, among which sometimes even a human being becomes a victim by the brigandage of a priest, while blood, caught warm from the throat in a foaming dish, while it still seethes, and as if thrown into the face of a thirsty idol, is cruelly offered as a drink, and amid the pleasures of the spectators the death of certain people is dispensed, so that through the bloody show one learns to be savage, as if a person's own private madness were too little, unless he learns it also publicly. For the punishment of a human being a raging wild beast is nourished amid delights, so that under the eyes of the spectators it may rage more cruelly. The trainer instructs the beast, which perhaps would have been more harmless, if a crueler teacher had not taught it to be savage. Therefore, to be silent about whatever idolatry proves more broadly, how vain are the contests themselves: quarrels over colors, contentions over chariots, partisanship over honors, to rejoice that a horse was swifter, to grieve that it was slower, to count the years of the animal, to know the consuls, to learn the ages, to point out the lineage, to recall the grandfathers and great-great-grandfathers themselves. How utterly idle is this business, indeed how shamefully disgraceful? This man, I say, who from memory counts the whole offspring of the horse family and without stumbling recounts this lineage with great speed, if you ask him the parents of Christ, he does not know, or more wretched if he does know. If you ask him again by what route he arrived at that show, he will confess through the brothel, through the naked bodies of prostitutes, through slippery lust, through public disgrace, through common wantonness, through the shared insult of all. To whom, so that I may not reproach him for what he perhaps committed, he nevertheless saw what ought not to have been committed and led his eyes to the show of idolatry through lust: he dared to lead the holy thing with him into the brothel, if he could have, who, hurrying to the show, dismissed from the Lord's house and still carrying with him, as is customary, the Eucharist among the obscene bodies of prostitutes, this unfaithful man carried around the holy body of Christ, deserving more condemnation from the route than from the pleasure of the show.

choices.english: by the brigandage of a priest
choices.why: Keeps the violent, criminal force of latrocinium, which is stronger than mere 'act' or 'crime'; the priest is a robber-murderer.
Patera is a broad sacrificial dish; 'foaming' preserves the vivid physical detail of warm blood.

choices.term: quasi sitienti idolo in faciem iactatus
choices.english: as if thrown into the face of a thirsty idol
choices.why: Keeps the contemptuous 'as if' and the mockery of the idol as thirsty; iactatus is violent throwing.
rejected: hurled at a thirsting idol's face

choices.why: Required glossary rendering; the literal route to the circus is a brothel district.

choices.term: ausus secum sanctum in lupanar ducere
choices.english: he dared to lead the holy thing with him into the brothel
choices.why: Sanctum is neuter, referring to the consecrated Eucharist, not a person; 'holy thing' preserves the grammatical and theological point.
rejected: he dared to take the Holy One with him
he dared to bring the holy into the brothel

choices.why: Infidelis is a strong term of condemnation, not just 'unbelieving'; 'carried around' keeps the motion of circumtulit.

pass_b_english: Why should I go on at length describing the monstrous kinds of sacrifices that take place in the games? Sometimes a human being even becomes the sacrificial victim through the brigandage of a priest, when blood still warm from the throat is caught in a foaming dish and, while it still steams, is thrown as if into the face of a thirsty idol and cruelly offered as a drink. And amid the pleasures of the spectators, someone's death is dispensed, so that through a bloody spectacle people learn to be savage—as if a person's private rage were not enough unless he also learns it in public. For the punishment of a human being, a raging wild beast is fed as a luxury, so that under the spectators' eyes it may rage more cruelly. The trainer schools the beast, which perhaps would have been less mad if a crueler master had not taught it to be savage.

So, to say nothing of all that idolatry proves, how vain these things are in themselves. Contests, quarrels over colors, rivalries over chariots, partisanship over honors—rejoicing that one horse was faster, grieving that another was slower, counting the years of the animal, knowing the consuls under which it raced, learning the ages, designating the lineage, recalling the grandfathers and great-great-grandfathers themselves. How utterly idle is this business—no, how shamefully disgraceful! Ask this man, I say, who from memory counts the whole offspring of the horse family and recites this lineage at great speed without stumbling, ask him about the parents of Christ, and he does not know—or he is more unfortunate if he does know. And if I ask him again by what route he arrived at that public show, he will confess: through the brothel, past the naked bodies of prostitutes, through slippery lust, through public disgrace, through common wantonness, through the shared insult of everyone. I will not charge him with what he perhaps did, but he certainly saw what should not have been done, and he led his eyes to the spectacle of idolatry through lust. He dared to lead the holy thing with him into the brothel—if he could have, this unfaithful man, hurrying to the public show after being dismissed from the Lord's house and still carrying with him, as is customary, the Eucharist, carried around the holy body of Christ among the obscene bodies of prostitutes, deserving more condemnation from the journey than from the pleasure of the show.

last_rejected.quote: how vain these things are in themselves
last_rejected.why: Source asks 'how vain are they' (exclamatory quam), not 'how vain these things are'.
last_rejected.fix: how vain they are in themselves
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'quam vana sunt ipsa' = 'how vain they are'; English 'how vain these things are in themselves' conveys same meaning

problems.quote: through the brigandage of a priest
problems.why: 'Brigandage of a priest' is opaque; the context describes ritual human sacrifice but the phrase does not convey this clearly.
problems.fix: Rephrase, e.g. 'through the sacrificial violence of a priest'.

problems.quote: counting the years of the animal, knowing the consuls
problems.why: 'Knowing the consuls' in a list about horse-racing trivia likely means knowing the consuls under which a horse was born or raced, but as printed it reads oddly.
problems.fix: Add context: 'knowing the consuls [under which it raced]'.

edits.old: through the brigandage of a priest
edits.new: through the sacrificial violence of a priest
knowing the consuls under which it raced

fixed: Changed 'brigandage of a priest' to 'sacrificial violence of a priest' to clarify the ritual human sacrifice context (source: 'latrocinio sacerdotis').
Added 'under which it raced' after 'knowing the consuls' to clarify the horse-racing context (source: 'consules nosse').
